pumac-2019-finals-a-01.title: A decreasing invariant
pumac-2019-finals-a-01.body:
Let $|V|$, $|E|$ and $c$ be the numbers of vertices, edges and connected components. For any graph, each component with $n_i$ vertices has at least $n_i-1$ edges (it contains a spanning tree), so
$$\mu=|E|-|V|+c\ge0 .$$
Now look at one operation on a cycle $C$ of length $\ell$:
- $|E|$ is unchanged: we add $\ell$ edges $vx$ and delete the $\ell$ edges of $C$.
- $|V|$ increases by $1$.
- $c$ is unchanged: the new vertex $v$ is joined to the component containing $C$; each deleted edge $xy$ of $C$ is replaced by the path $x\,v\,y$, so any two vertices connected before are still connected, and no new connections between different old components arise.

Therefore $\mu$ decreases by exactly $1$ with each operation. Since $\mu$ starts at a finite value and can never be negative, at most $\mu(G)=|E|-|V|+c$ operations can be performed. ∎

pumac-2019-finals-a-01.title: Official sketch (connected case)
pumac-2019-finals-a-01.body: For a connected graph: the number of edges is constant, the graph stays connected, and the number of vertices increases by one each time. A connected graph has at least $|V|-1$ edges, so after at most $|E|-|V|+1$ operations we reach $|E|=|V|-1$; then the graph is a tree, which has no cycle, and no further operation is possible. For a disconnected graph apply the same argument to each component (an operation only involves one component). ∎

pumac-2019-finals-a-02.title: A polynomial congruence
pumac-2019-finals-a-02.body:
**Lemma.** If $u,v$ are polynomials with integer coefficients and $u\equiv v\pmod{p^k}$ (coefficientwise) for some $k\ge1$, then $u^p\equiv v^p\pmod{p^{k+1}}$.

*Proof.* Write $u=v+p^kt$. Then $u^p=v^p+\binom p1v^{p-1}p^kt+\sum_{i\ge2}\binom piv^{p-i}p^{ik}t^i$. The second term is divisible by $p^{k+1}$, and for $i\ge2$, $p^{ik}$ is divisible by $p^{2k}$, and $2k\ge k+1$. $\square$

Now $(1+x)^p=1+x^p+\sum_{i=1}^{p-1}\binom pix^i\equiv 1+x^p\pmod p$, since $p\mid\binom pi$ for $0<i<p$. Applying the lemma $m-1$ times,
$$(1+x)^{p^m}=\left((1+x)^p\right)^{p^{m-1}}\equiv(1+x^p)^{p^{m-1}}\pmod{p^m}.$$
The coefficient of $x^{pj}$ on the left is $\binom{p^m}{pj}$ and on the right is $\binom{p^{m-1}}{j}$. Hence $p^m\mid\binom{p^m}{pj}-\binom{p^{m-1}}{j}$. ∎

pumac-2019-finals-a-02.title: Split the product (official idea)
pumac-2019-finals-a-02.body:
Write $N=p^m$, $k=pj$ and $\binom Nk=\prod_{i=1}^{k}\frac{N-k+i}{i}$. The factors with $i=pt$ ($1\le t\le j$) give $\prod_{t=1}^j\frac{p^{m-1}-j+t}{t}=\binom{p^{m-1}}{j}$. The remaining factor is
$$R=\prod_{i\in I}\frac{p^m-(pj-i)}{i},\qquad I=\{1\le i<pj:\ p\nmid i\};$$
as $i\mapsto pj-i$ permutes $I$, $R=\frac{\prod_{i\in I}(p^m-i)}{\prod_{i\in I}i}=\frac{A}{B}$ with $p\nmid B$ and $A\equiv(-1)^{|I|}B\pmod{p^m}$, where $|I|=j(p-1)$.

So $B\left(\binom{p^m}{pj}-\binom{p^{m-1}}{j}\right)=\binom{p^{m-1}}{j}(A-B)$.
- If $p$ is odd, or $p=2$ with $j$ even, then $|I|$ is even, $p^m\mid A-B$, and since $p\nmid B$ we are done.
- If $p=2$ and $j$ is odd, then $2^m\mid A+B$, so $A-B\equiv-2B\pmod{2^m}$. Also $\binom{2^{m-1}}{j}=\frac{2^{m-1}}{j}\binom{2^{m-1}-1}{j-1}$ with $j$ odd, so $2^{m-1}\mid\binom{2^{m-1}}{j}$ and $2^m\mid 2B\binom{2^{m-1}}{j}$. Again $2^m$ divides the right side, hence the difference. ∎

pumac-2019-finals-a-03.title: Alternating sides and three parallelograms (official)
pumac-2019-finals-a-03.body:
**Step 1: longer and shorter sides alternate.** Colour a side red if it is longer than its opposite side and blue if shorter (never equal by hypothesis). Opposite sides get different colours. Suppose two adjacent sides, say $AB$ and $BC$, are red. One of the opposite pair $CD$, $FA$ is red; say $FA$ (the other case is symmetric). Project $F$ and $C$ onto line $AB$ at $F',C'$ and onto line $DE$ at $F'',C''$; since $AB\parallel DE$, $F'C'C''F''$ is a rectangle and $F'C'=F''C''$.

The triangles $AFF'$ and $DCC''$ have parallel corresponding sides ($AF\parallel DC$, $FF'\parallel CC''$, $AF'\parallel DC''$), so they are similar; as $AF>DC$, we get $AF'>DC''$. Likewise $BC>EF$ gives $BC'>EF''$. Because all angles are obtuse, the feet lie outside the sides, so
$$F'C'=F'A+AB+BC'>C''D+DE+EF''=C''F'',$$
using $AB>DE$ — a contradiction. So the colours alternate around the hexagon.

**Step 2: tiling.** Without loss of generality $AB$, $CD$, $EF$ are blue (shorter): $AB<DE$, $CD<FA$, $EF<BC$. Draw lines $k$ through $A$ parallel to $BC$, $l$ through $C$ parallel to $DE$, $m$ through $E$ parallel to $FA$, and let $X=k\cap l$, $Y=l\cap m$, $Z=m\cap k$. Then $ABCX$, $CDEY$, $EFAZ$ are parallelograms. Since $AZ=EF<BC=AX$, $Z$ lies between $A$ and $X$; similarly $X$ is between $C$ and $Y$, and $Y$ between $E$ and $Z$. Hence the hexagon is the union of the three parallelograms and the triangle $XYZ$ (non-degenerate), so
$$S=[ABCX]+[CDEY]+[EFAZ]+[XYZ]>2\left(A_{ABC}+A_{CDE}+A_{EFA}\right).$$

**Step 3.** Do the same at $B$, $D$, $F$: let $X'=B+D-C$, $Y'=D+F-E$, $Z'=F+B-A$, so $BCDX'$, $DEFY'$, $FABZ'$ are parallelograms. On the line through $B$ parallel to $CD$ we have $BX'=CD<FA=BZ'$, so $X'$ lies between $B$ and $Z'$; similarly $Y'$ lies between $D$ and $X'$ (as $EF<BC$) and $Z'$ between $F$ and $Y'$ (as $AB<DE$). This is the same non-overlapping pattern as in Step 2, so $S=[BCDX']+[DEFY']+[FABZ']+[X'Y'Z']>2(A_{BCD}+A_{DEF}+A_{FAB})$. Adding the two inequalities and dividing by $2$ yields the claim. ∎
